$=\int_0^{\pi / 2} \frac{\sin \left(\frac{\pi}{2}-x\right)}{\sin \left(\frac{\pi}{2}-x\right)+\cos \left(\frac{\pi}{2}-x\right)} d x$
On adding Eqs. (i) and (ii), we get $\begin{aligned} & 2 I_1=\int_0^{\pi / 2} 1 d x=\frac{\pi}{2} \\ & \Rightarrow \quad I_1=\frac{\pi}{4} \\ & \therefore \quad I=100\left[\frac{\pi}{2}+\frac{\pi}{4}\right]=100 \times \frac{3 \pi}{4}=75 \pi \\ & \end{aligned}$

8136.text: Which of the following is an improper rational fraction?
8136.sol:
For improper fraction $\left[\frac{p(x)}{q(x)}\right]$
(i) $P(x) and q(x)$ both are polynomial.
(ii) Degree of $p(x) \geq$ degree of $q(x)$.

Option (a) $\frac{x^2+1}{\left(x^2+1\right)\left(x^2+x+1\right)}=\frac{p(x)}{q(x)}$
Degree of $p(x)=2$
Degree of $q(x)=4$
It is not improper fraction.
Option (b) $\frac{x^2+1}{(x+3)\left(x^2-x+1\right)}=\frac{p(x)}{q(x)}$
Degree of $p(x)=\mathbf{2}$
Degree of $q(x)=32 \lt  3\therefore$ It is not improper fraction.
Option (c) $\frac{x}{x^2+3 x+1}=\frac{p(x)}{q(x)}$
Degree of $p(x)=1$
Degree of $q(x)=21 \lt  2\therefore$ It is not improper fraction.
Option (d) $\frac{p(x)}{q(x)}=\frac{x^2+1}{x^2-1}$
Degree of $p(x)=2=$ degree of $q(x)\therefore \mathrm{It}$ is improper fraction.

8182.text: If $- \dfrac{\pi}{4} < x < \dfrac{\pi}{4},$ then the general solution of the differential equation $\cos^{2}x \cdot \dfrac{dy}{dx} - ( tan2x ) y = \cos^{4}x$ is
8182.sol:
Given,

${cos}^{2}x \cdot \dfrac{dy}{dx} - ( tan2x ) y = {cos}^{4}x$

$⇒ \dfrac{dy}{dx} - \left(\dfrac{tan2x}{{cos}^{2}x}\right)y = \dfrac{{cos}^{4}x}{{cos}^{2}x}$

$⇒ \dfrac{dy}{dx} - \left(\dfrac{tan2x}{{cos}^{2}x}\right)y = {cos}^{2}x$

This is the linear differential equation of the form $\dfrac{dy}{dx} + Py = Q$. Therefore, we get

$P = - \left(\dfrac{tan2x}{{cos}^{2}x}\right)$ and $Q = {cos}^{2}x$

I.F. $= {e}^{∫ Pdx}$

Now, 

$∫ Pdx = - ∫ \left(\dfrac{tan2x}{{cos}^{2}x}\right)dx$

             $= - ∫ \left(\dfrac{2tanx}{1 - {tan}^{2}x}\right){sec}^{2}xdx$

Let $tanx = t ⇒ {sec}^{2}xdx = dt$

$∫ Pdx = ∫ \left(\dfrac{- 2t}{1 - {t}^{2}}\right)dt$

              $= {\log}_{e}\left|1 - {t}^{2}\right|$

${e}^{∫ Pdx} = {e}^{{\log}_{e}\left|1 - {tan}^{2}x\right|} = \left(1 - {tan}^{2}x\right)$

Now, the solution of the linear differential equation is

$y \times I . F . = ∫ \left(I . F . \times Q\right)dx + C$

$⇒ y\left(1 - {tan}^{2}x\right) = ∫ \left\{\left(1 - {tan}^{2}x\right){cos}^{2}x\right\}dx + C$

$⇒ y\left(1 - {tan}^{2}x\right) = ∫ \left\{{cos}^{2}x - {sin}^{2}x\right\}dx + C$

$⇒ y\left(1 - {tan}^{2}x\right) = ∫ cos2xdx + C$

$⇒ y\left(1 - {tan}^{2}x\right) = \dfrac{sin2x}{2} + \dfrac{c}{2}$

$⇒ y = \dfrac{1}{2}\left\{\dfrac{sin2x + c}{\left(1 - {tan}^{2}x\right)}\right\}$

15808.sol: Given Data: Initial velocity, $u=10 \mathrm{~m} / \mathrm{s}$ Angle of projection, $\theta=60^{{}^{\circ}}$ Radius of curvature at $t=1 s$ is $R$ Acceleration due to gravity, $g=10 \mathrm{~m} / \mathrm{s}$ Finding the radius of curvature: Resolving the velocity into $x and y$ components, at any time $t\begin{aligned}$& v_x=u \cos 60^{{}^{\circ}}=10 $\times \frac{1}{2}$\\ & v_x=5 $\mathrm{~m}$/ $\mathrm{s}$\\ & v_y=u \sin 60^{{}^{\circ}}+a t=$\frac{10 \sqrt{3}}{2}-$10 t \\ & v_y=|5 $\sqrt{3}-$10 t| \end{aligned} $$ \\ At $t=1 s$ v_y=|5 $\sqrt{3}-$10| Angle made by body with respect to horizontal axis at $t=1 \mathrm{~s}\begin{aligned}$& \tan $\alpha=\left|\frac{v_y}{v_x}\right|=\left|\frac{5 \sqrt{3}-10}{5}\right|,$\\ & \tan $\alpha==|\sqrt{3}-$2| \\ & $\alpha=\tan ^{-1}(|\sqrt{3}-$2|)=15^{{}^{\circ}} \end{aligned}$ The radius of curvature same as range at timet$, which is given by $\begin{aligned}$R & =$\frac{v^2}{g \cos \alpha}=\frac{v_x^2+v_y^2}{g \cos \alpha}$\\ R & =$\frac{5^2+(5 \sqrt{3}-10)^2}{10 \times \cos 15^o}$\\ R & =$\frac{25+75+100-100 \sqrt{3}}{10 \times \cos 15^{{}^{\circ}}}$\\ R & =$\frac{26.79}{9.65}=$2.77 \\ R & =2.77 m $\approx$2.8 m \end{aligned} Hence, option $C$ is correct

19554.subject: Chemistry
19554.text: Two statements, one Assertion (A) and the other Reason (R) are given. Choose the correct option. Assertion: Compound $[\mathrm{X}]$ reacts with Hydrazine in presence of $\mathrm{KOH} /$ Glycol to form the product $[\mathrm{Y}]$.
options: Both A and R are correct and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both $A$ and $R$ are correct but $R$ is not the correct explanation of $A$.
A is wrong but R is correct.
19554.sol:
The reaction shown is the Wolff-Kishner reduction, which uses hydrazine (NH_{2}NH_{2}$) in the presence of a strong base like $KOH$ and a high-boiling solvent like ethylene glycol to reduce a carbonyl group (aldehyde or ketone) to a methylene group ($-CH_{2}-$).

In the given reaction, the aldehyde group ($-CHO$) in compound [X] is reduced to a methyl group ($-CH_{3}$) to form compound [Y].

The Wolff-Kishner reduction is specifically designed to reduce carbonyl compounds to alkanes. It does not affect other functional groups like alkyl halides under standard conditions, although strong bases like $KOH$ can potentially cause elimination reactions in alkyl halides. However, in the context of this transformation, the conversion of the aldehyde to the methyl group is the primary intended reaction.

Since the assertion correctly describes the transformation of [X] to [Y] using the Wolff-Kishner reduction conditions, and the reaction is indeed a standard application of this named reaction, the assertion is correct.

Answer: Both A and R are correct and R is the correct explanation of A.$

19655.text: A polysaccharide $[\mathrm{X}]$ represented as $\left(\mathrm{C}_6 \mathrm{H}_{10} \mathrm{O}_5\right)$ n serves as a reserve carbohydrate in human beings. An enzyme Phosphorylase breaks it down to glucose when required. It is also found in yeast and fungi. What is $[\mathrm{X}]$ ?
19655.sol:
The polysaccharide represented by the formula $(\mathrm{C}_6 \mathrm{H}_{10} \mathrm{O}_5)_n$ is a polymer of glucose. Among the given options, glycogen is the primary reserve carbohydrate in humans and animals, stored mainly in the liver and muscles. It is also known as animal starch and is found in yeast and fungi. Glycogen is broken down into glucose-1-phosphate by the enzyme glycogen phosphorylase during glycogenolysis to meet the body's energy requirements. Cellulose is a structural polysaccharide in plants, while starch and amylose are reserve carbohydrates in plants.

Answer: Glycogen

20246.text:
A statement of Assertion followed by a statement of Reason is given. Choose the correct answer out of the following options.
Assertion: The Eclipsed and the Staggered conformations of Ethane continuously flip from one form to the other. Reason: The torsional barrier between the Conformers of Ethane has a high value of about $50 \mathrm{ kJ} / \mathrm{mol}$ and this restricts free rotation around $\mathrm{C}-\mathrm{C}$ bond.
options: Both Assertion and Reason are correct and Reason is the correct explanation of Assertion.
Assertion is incorrect but Reason is correct statement.
Both Assertion and Reason are incorrect statements.
Assertion is correct but Reason is incorrect statement.
20246.sol:
The eclipsed and staggered conformations of ethane are conformers that interconvert rapidly at room temperature due to the low energy barrier for rotation around the carbon-carbon single bond. Thus, the assertion that they continuously flip is correct.

The torsional barrier for rotation in ethane is approximately $12.5 \text{ kJ/mol}$ (or $3 \text{ kcal/mol}$), not $50 \text{ kJ/mol}$. This energy barrier is low enough to allow for rapid rotation at room temperature, meaning rotation is not restricted. Therefore, the reason provided is incorrect.

Answer: Assertion is correct but Reason is incorrect statement.

20451.text: The ionisation constant of the weak acid HF whose concentration is $0.1\text{ M}$ is $3.5 \times 10^{-4}$. The Equilibrium constant value for the reaction $\text{F}^- + \text{H}_2\text{O} \rightleftharpoons \text{HF} + \text{OH}^-$ is _____ and the pH of aqueous solution of the weak acid is _____.
20451.sol:
The reaction $F^- + H_2O \rightleftharpoons HF + OH^-$ is hydrolysis of the conjugate base, so $K_{eq} = K_b = \dfrac{K_w}{K_a}$:

$K_{eq} = \dfrac{1.0 \times 10^{-14}}{3.5 \times 10^{-4}} \approx 2.86 \times 10^{-11}$

For pH, using $[H^+] \approx \sqrt{K_a \cdot C}$:

$[H^+] = \sqrt{3.5 \times 10^{-4} \times 0.1} = \sqrt{3.5 \times 10^{-5}} \approx 5.92 \times 10^{-3}$ M

$pH = -\log(5.92 \times 10^{-3}) \approx 2.23$

20671.subject: Chemistry
20671.text: What would be the van't Hoff factor for a solution prepared by dissolving $3.42 \mathrm{ g}$ of $\mathrm{CaCl}_2$ in $2500 \mathrm{ ml}$ of water having an Osmotic pressure equal to $0.75 \mathrm{ atm}$. at $27^{{}^{\circ}} \mathrm{C}$ ? Molar mass of $\mathrm{CaCl}_2=111 \mathrm{ amu}$.
20671.sol:
The osmotic pressure formula is given by $\pi = iCRT$, where $i$ is the van't Hoff factor, $C$ is the molar concentration, $R$ is the gas constant, and $T$ is the temperature in Kelvin.

Given values:
Mass of $\text{CaCl}_{2} = 3.42 \text{ g}$
Molar mass of $\text{CaCl}_{2} = 111 \text{ g/mol}$
Volume of solution $V = 2500 \text{ ml} = 2.5 \text{ L}$
Osmotic pressure $\pi = 0.75 \text{ atm}$
Temperature $T = 27^{{}^{\circ}}\text{C} = 300 \text{ K}$
Gas constant $R = 0.0821 \text{ L atm K}^{-1} \text{ mol}^{-1}$

Calculate the number of moles of $\text{CaCl}_{2}$:
$n = \dfrac{3.42}{111} \approx 0.03081 \text{ mol}$

Calculate the molar concentration $C$:
$C = \dfrac{n}{V} = \dfrac{0.03081}{2.5} = 0.012324 \text{ M}$

Using the osmotic pressure equation $\pi = iCRT$:
$0.75 = i \times 0.012324 \times 0.0821 \times 300$

$0.75 = i \times 0.303586$

$i = \dfrac{0.75}{0.303586} \approx 2.47$

Answer: 2.47

21492.subject: Mathematics
21492.text: $The distance between the foci of a hyperbola is 16 and its eccentricity is \sqrt{2}$. Then its equation is
21492.sol:
The distance between the foci of a hyperbola is given by $2ae = 16$.

Given the eccentricity $e = \sqrt{2}$, we have $2a\sqrt{2} = 16$, which simplifies to $a\sqrt{2} = 8$, so $a = \dfrac{8}{\sqrt{2}} = 4\sqrt{2}$.

Squaring $a$, we get $a^2 = (4\sqrt{2})^2 = 16 \times 2 = 32$.

For a hyperbola, the relationship between $a, b,$ and $e$ is $b^2 = a^2(e^2 - 1)$.

Substituting the known values, $b^2 = 32((\sqrt{2})^2 - 1) = 32(2 - 1) = 32$.

The standard equation of a hyperbola centered at the origin is $\dfrac{x^2}{a^2} - \dfrac{y^2}{b^2} = 1$.

Substituting $a^2 = 32$ and $b^2 = 32$, we get $\dfrac{x^2}{32} - \dfrac{y^2}{32} = 1$, which simplifies to $x^2 - y^2 = 32$.

Answer: $x^2-y^2=32$

21648.sol:
Let $x = \dfrac{\pi}{2} - \theta$. As $\theta \rightarrow \dfrac{\pi}{2}$, $x \rightarrow 0$.

Substituting $\theta = \dfrac{\pi}{2} - x$, we have $\sin \theta = \sin(\dfrac{\pi}{2} - x) = \cos x$ and $\cos \theta = \cos(\dfrac{\pi}{2} - x) = \sin x$.

The limit becomes $\lim_{x \rightarrow 0} \dfrac{1 - \cos x}{x \sin x}$.

Using the identity $1 - \cos x = 2 \sin^2(\dfrac{x}{2})$, the expression is $\lim_{x \rightarrow 0} \dfrac{2 \sin^2(\dfrac{x}{2})}{x \sin x}$.

Dividing numerator and denominator by $x^2$, we get $\lim_{x \rightarrow 0} \dfrac{2 \left(\dfrac{\sin(x/2)}{x}\right)^2}{\dfrac{\sin x}{x}} = \lim_{x \rightarrow 0} \dfrac{2 \left(\dfrac{1}{2} \cdot \dfrac{\sin(x/2)}{x/2}\right)^2}{\dfrac{\sin x}{x}}$.

Since $\lim_{x \rightarrow 0} \dfrac{\sin x}{x} = 1$, the limit is $\dfrac{2 \cdot (1/2)^2}{1} = \dfrac{2}{4} = \dfrac{1}{2}$.

Answer: $\dfrac{1}{2}$

22608.text: A $500 \mathrm{ W}$ heating unit is designed to operate on a $400 \mathrm{ V}$ line. If line voltage drops to $160 \mathrm{ V}$, the percentage drop in heat output will be:
22608.sol:
The power $P$ consumed by a heating unit is given by the formula $P = \dfrac{V^2}{R}$, where $V$ is the voltage and $R$ is the resistance of the heating element.

Since the resistance $R$ is constant, the power is proportional to the square of the voltage, $P \propto V^2$.

Let $P_1 = 500 \text{ W}$ at $V_1 = 400 \text{ V}$. When the voltage drops to $V_2 = 160 \text{ V}$, the new power $P_2$ is given by:

$\dfrac{P_2}{P_1} = \left( \dfrac{V_2}{V_1} \right)^2$

Substituting the values:

$\dfrac{P_2}{500} = \left( \dfrac{160}{400} \right)^2 = \left( \dfrac{2}{5} \right)^2 = \dfrac{4}{25}$

$P_2 = 500 \times \dfrac{4}{25} = 20 \times 4 = 80 \text{ W}$

The drop in heat output is $P_1 - P_2 = 500 - 80 = 420 \text{ W}$.

The percentage drop in heat output is $\dfrac{P_1 - P_2}{P_1} \times 100 = \dfrac{420}{500} \times 100 = \dfrac{420}{5} = 84\%$.

Answer: 84%

22788.subject: Physics
22788.text: Two point charges $P = +25\ \mu C$ and $Q = -16\ \mu C$ are placed 5 cm apart. Find the position of the point at which the resultant electric field is zero:
options: 2.5cm from Q and 2.5cm from P on the dipole axis
1cm from Q and 4cm from P on the dipole axis
20cm from Q and 25cm from P on the dipole axis
25cm from Q and 20cm from P on the dipole axis
22788.sol:
Let the point where the electric field is zero be at a distance $x$ from charge $Q$. Since the charges are of opposite signs, the null point lies outside the region between the charges, closer to the charge with the smaller magnitude ($Q$).

Distance of the point from $Q = x$
Distance of the point from $P = x + 5$

For the net electric field to be zero, the magnitudes of the electric fields due to both charges must be equal:

$\dfrac{k|P|}{(x+5)^2} = \dfrac{k|Q|}{x^2}$

Substituting the given values:

$\dfrac{k \times 25}{(x+5)^2} = \dfrac{k \times 16}{x^2}$

Taking the square root on both sides:

$\dfrac{5}{x+5} = \dfrac{4}{x}$

$5x = 4(x+5)$

$5x = 4x + 20$

$x = 20$ cm

The distance from $Q$ is $20$ cm and the distance from $P$ is $20 + 5 = 25$ cm.

Answer: 20cm from Q and 25cm from P on the dipole axis

22966.subject: Physics
22966.text: Pick out the weakest force from the four given fundamental forces in nature.
22966.sol:
The four fundamental forces in nature are the strong nuclear force, the electromagnetic force, the weak nuclear force, and the gravitational force.

The relative strengths of these forces are typically compared by considering the interaction between two protons at a distance of $10^{-15}$ m. The strong nuclear force is the strongest, followed by the electromagnetic force, then the weak nuclear force, and finally the gravitational force.

The gravitational force is the weakest among the four fundamental forces, as its coupling constant is extremely small compared to the others.

Answer: Gravitational force

28013.subject: Chemistry
28013.text:
For the following reaction at $50°$C and at $2$ atm pressure,
$2N_2O_5(g) \rightleftharpoons 2N_2O_4(g)+O_2(g)$
$N_2O_5$ is $50\%$ dissociated.
The magnitude of standard free energy change at this temperature is $x$.
$x=$ ______ J mol$^{-1}$ [Nearest integer].
Given: $R=8.314$ J mol$^{-1}$ K$^{-1}$, $\log 2=0.30$, $\log 3=0.48$, $\ln 10=2.303$, $°C+273=K$
28013.sol:
Let the initial moles of $N_2O_5$ be $2$.

The given reaction is:
$2N_2O_5(g) \rightleftharpoons 2N_2O_4(g) + O_2(g)$

Since $N_2O_5$ is $50\%$ dissociated (degree of dissociation $\alpha = 0.5$), the moles at equilibrium are:
Moles of $N_2O_5 = 2(1 - 0.5) = 1$
Moles of $N_2O_4 = 2(0.5) = 1$
Moles of $O_2 = 0.5$

Total moles at equilibrium $= 1 + 1 + 0.5 = 2.5$

Given the total pressure $P = 2$ atm, the partial pressures of the gases are:
$P_{N_2O_5} = \dfrac{1}{2.5} \times 2 = 0.8$ atm
$P_{N_2O_4} = \dfrac{1}{2.5} \times 2 = 0.8$ atm
$P_{O_2} = \dfrac{0.5}{2.5} \times 2 = 0.4$ atm

The equilibrium constant $K_p$ is:
$K_p = \dfrac{(P_{N_2O_4})^2 \cdot P_{O_2}}{(P_{N_2O_5})^2} = \dfrac{(0.8)^2 \times 0.4}{(0.8)^2} = 0.4$

The standard free energy change $\Delta G^\circ$ is given by:
$\Delta G^\circ = -RT \ln K_p$

Using the given values:
$\ln(0.4) = 2.303 \log(0.4) = 2.303 (\log 4 - \log 10)$
$\ln(0.4) = 2.303 (2 \log 2 - 1) = 2.303 (2 \times 0.30 - 1) = 2.303 (-0.4) = -0.9212$

Now, substituting the values into the $\Delta G^\circ$ equation ($T = 50^\circ C + 273 = 323$ K):
$\Delta G^\circ = -8.314 \times 323 \times (-0.9212)$
$\Delta G^\circ = 2473.81$ J mol$^{-1}$

The magnitude of the standard free energy change to the nearest integer is $2474$ J mol$^{-1}$.

Answer: $2474$

30902.subject: Chemistry
30902.text:
Given below are two statements :

Statement I: Group $13$ trivalent halides get easily hydrolysed by water due to their covalent nature.

Statement II: ${AlCl}_{3}$ upon hydrolysis in acidified aqueous solution forms octahedral ${\left[Al{\left({H}_{2}O\right)}_{6}\right]}^{3 +}$ ion.

In the light of the above statements, choose the correct answer from the options given below :
options: Statement I is true but statement II is false
Statement I is false but statement II is true
Both statement I and statement II are false
Both statement I and statement II are true
30902.sol:
In trivalent state most of the 13th group compounds being covalent are hydrolysed in water. Trichlorides of group 13 on hydrolysis in water form tetrahedral ${\left[M{\left(OH\right)}_{4}\right]}^{-}$ species, the hybridisation state of element $M$ is ${sp}^{3}$.

In case of aluminium, acidified aqueous solution forms octahedral ${\left[Al{\left({H}_{2}O\right)}_{6}\right]}^{3 +}$ ion, which has an aluminium as a central metal atom and water molecules as ligands. The aluminium is in $+ 3$  oxidation state and forms$6{sp}^{3}{d}^{2}$ hybrid orbitals. 

Hence option D is the answer.

33650.subject: Mathematics
33650.text: Two tangents are drawn from a point $P$ to the circle ${x}^{2} + {y}^{2} - 2x - 4y + 4 = 0$, such that the angle between these tangents is $\tan^{- 1}\left(\dfrac{12}{5}\right)$, where $\tan^{- 1}\left(\dfrac{12}{5}\right) \in ( 0, \pi ) .$ If the centre of the circle is denoted by $C$ and these tangents touch the circle at points $A$ and $B$, then the ratio of the areas of $\DeltaPAB$ and $\DeltaCAB$ is :
33650.sol:
Let, the angle between the tangents $PA$ and $PB$ from the point $P$ to the circle ${x}^{2} + {y}^{2} - 2x - 4y + 4 = 0$ with centre $C$ is $\theta .$

Given $\theta = \tan^{- 1}\left(\dfrac{12}{5}\right) ⇒ tan\theta = \dfrac{12}{5} .$

We know that the centre and radius of a circle ${x}^{2} + {y}^{2} + 2gx + 2fy + c = 0$ are respectively $\left(- g, - f\right)$ and $\sqrt{{g}^{2} + {f}^{2} - c} .$

Thus, the centre and radius of the circle ${x}^{2} + {y}^{2} - 2x - 4y + 4 = 0$ are respectively $\left(1, 2\right)$ and $\sqrt{{1}^{2} + {2}^{2} - 4} = 1$ unit.

We know that the line joining the centre of a circle to the point of contact of the tangent is perpendicular to the tangent, hence $∠ CAP = ∠ CBP = 90 °$ also $CP$ bisects the angle $∠ APB$ as $∆ CAP ≅ ∆ CBP$ by $SSS$ congruency.

Thus, we have $∠ CPA = ∠ CPB = \dfrac{\theta}{2}$

In $∆ CAP,$ we have $tan\left(\dfrac{\theta}{2}\right) = \dfrac{AC}{AP}$

$⇒ tan\left(\dfrac{\theta}{2}\right) = \dfrac{1}{AP}$

$⇒ AP = cot\left(\dfrac{\theta}{2}\right)$

Now, area of $\DeltaPAB = \dfrac{1}{2}\left(PA\right)\left(PB\right)sin\theta$

Since, tangents to a circle from an external point are equal, hence $PA = PB$

Area of $\DeltaPAB = \dfrac{1}{2}{\left(PA\right)}^{2}sin\theta$

$= \dfrac{1}{2}co{t}^{2}\left(\dfrac{\theta}{2}\right)sin\theta$

$= \dfrac{1}{2}\dfrac{\cos^{2}\left(\dfrac{\theta}{2}\right)}{\sin^{2}\left(\dfrac{\theta}{2}\right)}sin\theta$

Using $cos2x = 2\cos^{2}x - 1 = 1 - 2\sin^{2}x,$ we get

Area of $\DeltaPAB = \dfrac{1}{2}\left(\dfrac{1 + cos\theta}{1 - cos\theta}\right)sin\theta$

We have $tan\theta = \dfrac{12}{5} ⇒ sin\theta = \dfrac{12}{13} \text{ and } cos\theta = \dfrac{5}{13}$

Area of $\DeltaPAB = \dfrac{1}{2}\left(\dfrac{1 + \dfrac{5}{13}}{1 - \dfrac{5}{13}}\right)\left(\dfrac{12}{13}\right)$

$= \dfrac{1}{2} \times \dfrac{18}{8} \times \dfrac{12}{13} = \dfrac{27}{26}$ sq units.

And, area of $\DeltaCAB = \dfrac{1}{2}\left(AC\right)\left(BC\right)sin\left(\pi - \theta\right)$

$= \dfrac{1}{2}sin\theta = \dfrac{1}{2}\left(\dfrac{12}{13}\right) = \dfrac{6}{13}$ sq units.

$∴\dfrac{areaof\DeltaPAB}{areaof\DeltaCAB} = \dfrac{\left(\dfrac{27}{26}\right)}{\left(\dfrac{6}{13}\right)} = \dfrac{9}{4} .$

34526.subject: Mathematics
34526.text:
The values of $a$ and $b$, for which the system of equations

$2x + 3y + 6z = 8$

$x + 2y + az = 5$

$3x + 5y + 9z = b$

has no solution, are :
34526.sol:
The given equation is

$2x + 3y + 6z = 8$

$x + 2y + az = 5$

$3x + 5y + 9z = b$

So, $D = \left|\begin{cases}2 & 3 & 6 \\ 1 & 2 & a \\ 3 & 5 & 9\end{cases}\right|$

$= 2\left(18 - 5a\right) - 3\left(9 - 3a\right) + 6\left(5 - 6\right)$

$= 36 - 10a - 27 + 9a + 30 - 36$

$= 3 - a$

${D}_{z} = \left|\begin{cases}2 & 3 & 8 \\ 1 & 2 & 5 \\ 3 & 5 & b\end{cases}\right|$

$= 2\left(2b - 10\right) - 3\left(b - 15\right) + 8\left(5 - 6\right)$

$= 4b - 20 - 3b + 15 + 40 - 48$

$= b - 13$

The system of equation has no solution if $D = 0 \text{ and } {D}_{z} \ne 0$

So, If $a = 3, b \ne 13$, then the system of equation has no solution.

34608.subject: Mathematics
34608.text:
If $a, b, c$ are non - zero real numbers and if the system of equations

$\left(a - 1\right)x = y + z$

$\left(b - 1\right)y = x + z$

$\left(c - 1\right)z = x + y$

has a non - trivial solution, then $ab + bc + ca$ equals :
34608.sol:
Given, $\left(a - 1\right)x = y + z ⇒ \left(a - 1\right)x - y - z = 0$

$\left(b - 1\right)y = z + x ⇒ - x + \left(b - 1\right)y - z = 0$

$\left(c - 1\right)z = y + x = - x - y + \left(c - 1\right)z = 0$

For a non-trivial solution

$\left|\begin{cases}a - 1 & - 1 & - 1 \\ - 1 & b - 1 & - 1 \\ - 1 & - 1 & c - 1\end{cases}\right| = 0$

$⇒ \left|\begin{cases}1 - a & 1 & 1 \\ 1 & 1 - b & 1 \\ 1 & 1 & 1 - c\end{cases}\right| = 0$

$⇒ \left(1 - a\right)\left[\left(1 - b\right)\left(1 - c\right) - 1\right] - 1\left[\left(1 - c\right) - 1\right] + \left[1 - \left(1 - b\right)\right] = 0$

$⇒ 1 - \left(a + b + c\right) + \left(ab + bc + ca\right) - abc - 1 + \left(a + b + c\right) = 0$

$⇒ ab + bc + ca = abc$

Given,

$f\left(x\right) = \left[1 + x\right] + \dfrac{{\alpha}^{2\left[x\right] + \left\{x\right\}} + \left[x\right] - 1}{2\left[x\right] + \left\{x\right\}}$

$\lim_{x \to {0}^{-}}\left[1 + x\right] + \dfrac{{\alpha}^{\left[x\right] + \left[x\right] + \left\{x\right\}} + \left[x\right] - 1}{2\left[x\right] + \left\{x\right\}} = \alpha - \dfrac{4}{3}$

36994.text: The quadratic equations $x^2-6 x+a=0$ and $x^2-c x+6=0$ have one root in common. The other roots of the first and second equations are integers in the ratio $4: 3$. Then the common root is
36994.sol:
Let $\alpha$ and $4 \beta$ be roots of $x^2-6 x+a=0$ and $\alpha, 3 \beta$ be the roots of $x^2-c x+6=0$, then $\alpha+4 \beta=6$ and $4 \alpha \beta=a$
$\alpha+3 \beta=c$ and $3 \alpha \beta=6$.
We get $\alpha \beta=2 \Rightarrow a=8$
So the first equation is $x^2-6 x+8=0 \Rightarrow x=2,4$
If $\alpha=2$ and $4 \beta=4$ then $3 \beta=3$
If $\alpha=4$ and $4 \beta=2$, then $3 \beta=3 / 2 \quad$ (non-integer)
$\therefore$ common root is $x=2$.

37214.text: For $k \in N,$ let $\dfrac{1}{\alpha ( \alpha + 1 ) ( \alpha + 2 ) \ldots \ldots . ( \alpha + 20 )} = \mathop{∑}_{K = 0}^{20}\dfrac{{A}_{k}}{\alpha + k},$ where $\alpha > 0 .$ Then the value of $100{\left(\dfrac{{A}_{14} + {A}_{15}}{{A}_{13}}\right)}^{2}$ is equal to ____________.
37214.sol:
We have,

$\mathop{∑}_{k = 0}^{20}\left(\dfrac{{A}_{k}}{\alpha + k}\right) = \dfrac{1}{\alpha\left(\alpha + 1\right) \ldots \ldots \left(\alpha + 20\right)}$

$⇒ \dfrac{{A}_{0}}{\alpha} + \dfrac{{A}_{1}}{\alpha + 1} + . . . + \dfrac{{A}_{20}}{\alpha + 20} = \dfrac{1}{\alpha\left(\alpha + 1\right) \ldots \ldots \left(\alpha + 20\right)}$

$⇒ \dfrac{{A}_{0}\left(\alpha + 1\right)\left(\alpha + 2\right) \ldots \ldots \left(\alpha + 19\right)\left(\alpha + 20\right) + {A}_{2}\alpha\left(\alpha + 2\right) \ldots \ldots \left(\alpha + 19\right)\left(\alpha + 20\right) + . . . + {A}_{20}\alpha\left(\alpha + 1\right)\left(\alpha + 2\right) \ldots \ldots \left(\alpha + 19\right)}{\alpha\left(\alpha + 1\right)\left(\alpha + 2\right) \ldots \ldots \left(\alpha + 20\right)} = \dfrac{1}{\alpha\left(\alpha + 1\right)\left(\alpha + 2\right) \ldots \ldots \left(\alpha + 20\right)}$

$⇒ {A}_{0}\left[\left(\alpha + 1\right)\left(\alpha + 2\right) \ldots \ldots \left(\alpha + 19\right)\left(\alpha + 20\right)\right] + {A}_{2}\left[\alpha\left(\alpha + 2\right) \ldots \ldots \left(\alpha + 19\right)\left(\alpha + 20\right)\right] + . . . + {A}_{20}\left[\alpha\left(\alpha + 1\right)\left(\alpha + 2\right) \ldots \ldots \left(\alpha + 19\right)\right] = 1 . . . . \left(i\right)$

Hence, coefficient of ${A}_{13}$ is

$\alpha\left(\alpha + 1\right) \ldots \left(\alpha + 12\right)\left(\alpha + 14\right) \ldots \left(\alpha + 19\right)\left(\alpha + 20\right)$.

Similarly, coefficient of ${A}_{14}$ is

$\alpha\left(\alpha + 1\right) \ldots \left(\alpha + 13\right)\left(\alpha + 15\right) \ldots \left(\alpha + 19\right)\left(\alpha + 20\right)$

And, coefficient of ${A}_{15}$ is

$\alpha\left(\alpha + 1\right) \ldots \left(\alpha + 14\right)\left(\alpha + 16\right) \ldots \left(\alpha + 19\right)\left(\alpha + 20\right)$

Then, to find ${A}_{14}$, put $\alpha = - 14$ in $\left(i\right)$, then we get

${A}_{14} = \dfrac{1}{( - 14 ) ( - 13 ) \ldots . . ( - 1 ) ( 1 ) \ldots . . ( 6 )} = \dfrac{1}{14 ! \cdot 6 !}$

Similarly, putting $\alpha = - 15$, we get

${A}_{15} = \dfrac{1}{( - 15 ) ( - 14 ) \ldots \ldots ( - 1 ) ( 1 ) \ldots . . ( 5 )} = - \dfrac{1}{15 ! \cdot 5 !}$

And, putting $\alpha = - 13$, we get

${A}_{13} = \dfrac{1}{( - 13 ) \ldots \ldots ( - 1 ) ( 1 ) \ldots . . ( 7 )} = \dfrac{- 1}{13 ! \cdot 7 !}$

Hence,

$\dfrac{{A}_{14}}{{A}_{13}} = \dfrac{1}{14 ! \cdot 6 !} \times \left(- 13 ! \times 7 !\right) = \dfrac{- 7}{14} = - \dfrac{1}{2}$

$\dfrac{{A}_{15}}{{A}_{13}} = \left(- \dfrac{1}{15 ! \times 5 !}\right) \times \left(- 13 ! \times 7 !\right) = \dfrac{42}{15 \times 14} = \dfrac{1}{5}$

Then,

$100{\left(\dfrac{{A}_{14}}{{A}_{13}} + \dfrac{{A}_{15}}{{A}_{13}}\right)}^{2} = 100{\left(- \dfrac{1}{2} + \dfrac{1}{5}\right)}^{2} = 9$

37614.text: A data consists of $n$ observations: ${x}_{1}, {x}_{2}, \ldots , {x}_{n} .$ If $\mathop{∑}_{i = 1}^{n}{\left({x}_{i} + 1\right)}^{2} = 9n$ and $\mathop{∑}_{i = 1}^{n}{\left({x}_{i} - 1\right)}^{2} = 5n$, then the standard deviation of this data is
37614.sol:
Given:

$\mathop{∑}_{i = 1}^{n}{\left({x}_{i} + 1\right)}^{2} = 9n$

$⇒ \mathop{∑}_{i = 1}^{n}\left({x}_{i}^{2} + 2{x}_{i} + 1\right) = 9n . . . \left(1\right)$

And, $\mathop{∑}_{i = 1}^{n}{\left({x}_{i} - 1\right)}^{2} = 5n$

$⇒ \mathop{∑}_{i = 1}^{n}\left({x}_{i}^{2} - 2{x}_{i} + 1\right) = 5n . . . \left(2\right)$

Form $\left(1\right) + \left(2\right)$, we get

$\mathop{∑}_{i = 1}^{n}\left(2{x}_{i}^{2} + 2\right) = 14n$

$⇒ \mathop{∑}_{i = 1}^{n}{x}_{i}^{2} = 6n . . . \left(3\right)$

From $\left(1\right) - \left(2\right)$, we get

$⇒ \mathop{∑}_{i = 1}^{n}{x}_{i} = n . . . \left(4\right)$

$∴$ Variance, ${\sigma}^{2} = E\left({x}^{2}\right) - {\left(E\left(x\right)\right)}^{2}$

$⇒ {\sigma}^{2} = \dfrac{∑ {x}^{2}}{n} - \dfrac{∑ x}{n}$

$⇒ {\sigma}^{2} = \dfrac{6n}{n} - {\left(\dfrac{n}{n}\right)}^{2} = 6 - 1 = 5$

$∴$ Standard deviation, $\sigma = \sqrt{5}$.

39272.chapter: Center of Mass, Momentum and Collision
39272.text: A body of mass 14 kg initially at rest explodes and breaks into three fragments of masses in the ratio $2: 2: 3$. The two pieces of equal masses fly off perpendicular to each other with a speed of $18 \mathrm{~m} / \mathrm{s}$ each. The velocity of the heavier fragment is $\_\_\_\_$ $\mathrm{m} / \mathrm{s}$.
39272.sol:
From mass ratio 2:2:3 with total mass 14 kg: individual masses are 4 kg, 4 kg, and 6 kg.
Setting coordinate axes along the motion directions of the two equal fragments: fragment 1 has momentum $\vec{p_1} = 4 \times 18\hat{i} = 72\hat{i}$ kg⋅m/s, and fragment 2 has $\vec{p_2} = 4 \times 18\hat{j} = 72\hat{j}$ kg⋅m/s.
By momentum conservation, initially at rest: $\vec{p_1} + \vec{p_2} + \vec{p_3} = 0$, so $\vec{p_3} = -72\hat{i} - 72\hat{j}$ kg⋅m/s.
Velocity of 6 kg fragment: $\vec{v_3} = \frac{\vec{p_3}}{6} = -12\hat{i} - 12\hat{j}$ m/s.
Speed: $|\vec{v_3}| = \sqrt{144 + 144} = \sqrt{288} = 12\sqrt{2}$ m/s.

40949.text: The acceleration due to gravity on the earth's surface at the poles is $g$ and angular velocity of the earth about the axis passing through the pole is $\omega$. An object is weighed at the equator and at a height $h$ above the poles by using a spring balance. If the weights are found to be same, then $h$ is: ($h ≪ R$, where $R$ is the radius of the earth)
40949.sol:
Acceleration due to gravity at height $h$ above the pole

is given by

${g}_{h} = g\left(1 - \dfrac{2h}{R}\right) . . . ( 1 )$

Acceleration due to gravity at the equator due to rotation of the earth is given by

$g ' = g - {\omega}^{2}R\cos^{2}\lambda . . . ( 2 )$

At the equator, $\lambda = 0$

$⇒ g ' = g - {\omega}^{2}R . . . ( 3 )$

As both weights are equal, i.e.; ${g}_{h} = {g}^{'}$

From equation $( 1 )$ and $( 2 )$, we get,
$⇒ {\omega}^{2}R = \dfrac{2g}{R}h$
$∴ h = \dfrac{{R}^{2}{\omega}^{2}}{2g}$

41030.subject: Physics
41030.text: One gas of $n_1$ mole of molecules at temperature $T_1$, volume $V_1$, and pressure $P_1$, and another gas of $n_2$ mole of molecules at temperature $T_2$, volume $V_2$, and pressure $P_2$, are mixed resulting in pressure $P$ and volume $V$ of the mixture. The temperature of the mixture is _____.
41030.sol:
From the ideal gas equation, the number of moles of the first gas is $n_1 = \dfrac{P_1 V_1}{R T_1}$ and the number of moles of the second gas is $n_2 = \dfrac{P_2 V_2}{R T_2}$.

For the mixture, the total number of moles is $n = n_1 + n_2$.

Applying the ideal gas equation for the mixture:

$P V = n R T$

$T = \dfrac{P V}{n R}$

Substituting the values of $n_1$ and $n_2$:

$T = \dfrac{P V}{\left( \dfrac{P_1 V_1}{R T_1} + \dfrac{P_2 V_2}{R T_2} \right) R}$

$T = \dfrac{P V}{\dfrac{P_1 V_1}{T_1} + \dfrac{P_2 V_2}{T_2}}$

$T = \dfrac{T_1 T_2 P V}{P_1 V_1 T_2 + P_2 V_2 T_1}$

Answer: $T_1 T_2 PV/(T_2 P_1 V_1 + T_1 P_2 V_2)$

44103.text: $\left(P + \dfrac{a}{{V}^{2}}\right)\left(V - b\right) = RT$ represents the equation of state of some gases. Where $P$ is the pressure, $V$ is the volume, $T$ is the temperature and $a, b, R$ are the constants. The physical quantity, which has dimensional formula as that of $\dfrac{{b}^{2}}{a}$ , will be :
44103.sol:
According to the principle of dimensional homogeneity, the dimensions of each terms of a dimensional equation on both sides are the same.

So, dimension of $b$ and $V$ will be same, $\left[b\right] = \left[V\right]$

And dimension of $\dfrac{a}{{V}^{2}}$ and $P$ will be same, $\left[\dfrac{a}{{V}^{2}}\right] = \left[P\right]$

From above two relations, we have $\left[\dfrac{a}{{b}^{2}}\right] = \left[P\right]$

$∴ \left[\dfrac{{b}^{2}}{a}\right] = \dfrac{1}{\left[P\right]} = {\left[M{L}^{- 1}{T}^{- 2}\right]}^{- 1}$

Thus, $\left[{M}^{- 1}{L}^{1}{T}^{2}\right]$ is the dimension of compressibility.

46248.subject: Physics
46248.text: A rocket is intended to leave the Earth's gravitational field. The fuel in its main engine is a little less than the amount that is necessary and an auxiliary engine, (only capable of operating for a short time) has to be used as well. When is it best to switch on the auxiliary engine?
options: when the rocket has nearly stopped with respect to the Earth.
46248.sol:
The rocket has to reach the highest possible total energy. If the zero level of gravitational potential energy is 'infinitely' far away, then the energy of the rocket standing on the surface of the earth is negative. The energy released during the operation of the engines increases the total energy of the rocket, and the rocket can leave, the earth's gravitational field if the sum of its potential and kinetic energies becomes positive.
The energy released in the course of the operation of the principal and auxiliary engines increases the total energy of the rocket and its ejected combustion products by a fixed value; this increase is independent of the moment when the engines are scratched on. However, the speed at which the combustion products fall back to the earth does depend on the timing of the rocket's operations. Indeed, if the auxiliary engine starts working when the rocket is at a greater height, the combustion products fall further and their speed and total energy are higher when they hit the ground. This means that the sooner the auxiliary engine is switched on, the higher the energy ultimately acquired by the rocket. The same argument is valid for the principal engine, and if the only energy consideration apply, it is best to operate the engines for the shortest time and at the highest thrust.

48869.subject: Mathematics
48869.text: Integrating factor of the differential equation $(1 + x^2)\dfrac{dy}{dx} + xy = 1$ is
48869.sol:
The given differential equation is $(1 + x^2)\dfrac{dy}{dx} + xy = 1$

Dividing the entire equation by $(1 + x^2)$, we get:

$\dfrac{dy}{dx} + \dfrac{x}{1 + x^2}y = \dfrac{1}{1 + x^2}$

This is a linear differential equation of the form $\dfrac{dy}{dx} + P(x)y = Q(x)$, where $P(x) = \dfrac{x}{1 + x^2}$ and $Q(x) = \dfrac{1}{1 + x^2}$

The integrating factor (IF) is given by $e^{\int P(x) dx}$

$\int P(x) dx = \int \dfrac{x}{1 + x^2} dx$

Let $1 + x^2 = t$, then $2x dx = dt \Rightarrow x dx = \dfrac{dt}{2}$

$\int \dfrac{x}{1 + x^2} dx = \dfrac{1}{2} \int \dfrac{dt}{t} = \dfrac{1}{2} \log t = \dfrac{1}{2} \log(1 + x^2) = \log(\sqrt{1 + x^2})$

Therefore, the integrating factor is $e^{\log(\sqrt{1 + x^2})} = \sqrt{1 + x^2}$

Answer: $\sqrt{1 + x^2}$

55660.subject: Chemistry
55660.text: When sodium bicarbonate is added to an organic compound, brisk effervescences is evolved. This indicate the presence of which functional group.
55660.sol:
Sodium bicarbonate ($NaHCO_3$) is a weak base that reacts with compounds more acidic than carbonic acid ($H_2CO_3$).

Carboxylic acids ($-\text{COOH}$) react with sodium bicarbonate to produce sodium carboxylate, water, and carbon dioxide gas.

The reaction is given by:

$R-\text{COOH} + NaHCO_3 \rightarrow R-\text{COONa} + H_2O + CO_2 \uparrow$

The evolution of carbon dioxide ($CO_2$) gas is observed as brisk effervescence. This test is the standard qualitative test used to detect the presence of the carboxylic acid functional group in an organic compound.

Answer: $-\text{COOH}$

55782.subject: Chemistry
55782.text: Which of the following is more polar?
55782.sol:
Molecular polarity depends on bond electronegativity differences and molecular geometry, with the overall dipole moment determined by the vector sum of individual bond dipoles.

$\mathrm{H}_2 \mathrm{S}$ exhibits bent geometry with bond dipoles that do not cancel, yielding $\mu \approx 0.97 \text{ D}$.

$\mathrm{NH}_3$'s trigonal pyramidal structure and highly polar N-H bonds produce a large dipole moment of $\mu \approx 1.47 \text{ D}$, enhanced by the lone pair contribution.

For $\mathrm{NF}_3$, the opposing directions of the N-F bond dipoles and lone pair dipole partially cancel, resulting in $\mu \approx 0.23 \text{ D}$.

$\mathrm{CHCl}_3$ has asymmetric tetrahedral geometry with non-canceling dipoles, giving $\mu \approx 1.04 \text{ D}$.

Comparing values, $\mathrm{NH}_3$ possesses the largest dipole moment.

58008.subject: Chemistry
58008.text: Dissociation constant of 0.01 M weak acid is $10^{-4}$. What is percent dissociation of acid?
58008.sol:
Dissociation of a weak acid follows the equilibrium: $HA \rightleftharpoons H^+ + A^-$. Given initial concentration $C = 0.01\text{ M}$ and dissociation constant $K_a = 10^{-4}$, the degree of dissociation $\alpha$ is determined from the expression:
$K_a = \frac{C\alpha^2}{1-\alpha}$.

For weak acids, $\alpha$ is typically small, allowing the approximation $1 - \alpha \approx 1$, simplifying to:
$K_a \approx C\alpha^2$.

Solving for $\alpha$:
$\alpha^2 = \frac{K_a}{C} = \frac{10^{-4}}{0.01} = 10^{-2}$
$\alpha = \sqrt{10^{-2}} = 0.1$

Multiplying by 100 gives the percentage dissociation:
Percent dissociation $= 0.1 \times 100\% = 10\%$

While $\alpha = 0.1$ slightly challenges the approximation, exact calculation yields $\alpha \approx 0.095$, still closest to $10\%$ among standard options. The correct choice is thus $\boxed{\text{C}}$.

59890.subject: Chemistry
59890.text: For a reaction to be spontaneous at all temperatures, the values of enthalpy change and entropy change should be
59890.sol:
For a reaction to be spontaneous, the change in Gibbs free energy must be negative, i.e., $\Delta G < 0$.

The relationship between $\Delta G$, enthalpy change $\Delta H$, and entropy change $\Delta S$ is given by the Gibbs equation:

$\Delta G = \Delta H - T\Delta S$

Since absolute temperature $T$ is always positive, for $\Delta G$ to be negative at all temperatures, both terms contributing to $\Delta G$ must favor spontaneity. This happens when:

$\Delta H < 0$ (exothermic reaction)
$\Delta S > 0$ (increase in entropy)

Under these conditions, the term $-T\Delta S$ is negative, and since $\Delta H$ is also negative, their sum $\Delta G$ will always be negative regardless of the temperature.

Answer: $\Delta H < 0$ and $\Delta S > 0$

59944.subject: Chemistry
59944.text: Which from following process involves zero work done?
59944.sol:
The work done by a gas during expansion or compression is given by $W = -P_{ ext{ext}}\Delta V$, where $P_{ ext{ext}}$ is the external pressure and $\Delta V$ is the volume change.

Isobaric expansion occurs at constant pressure with $\Delta V eq 0$, yielding non-zero work since $P_{ ext{ext}} eq 0$.

Adiabatic compression involves volume decrease with no heat exchange, producing non-zero work as $P_{ ext{ext}} eq 0$.

Isothermal expansion maintains constant temperature with volume increase, resulting in non-zero work $W = -nRT \ln(V_2/V_1)$.

Free expansion occurs against zero external pressure ($P_{ ext{ext}} = 0$), making $W = 0$ regardless of $\Delta V$.

The process involving zero work is free expansion.

60588.subject: Mathematics
60588.text: The area of the region bounded by the curve $\mathrm{y}=|x-2|$ between $x=1, x=3$ and X -axis is......
60588.sol:
The area bounded by $y=|x-2|$ from $x=1$ to $x=3$ and the X-axis is found by evaluating $\int_{1}^{3} |x-2| dx$.

The piecewise definition of $|x-2|$ gives two subintervals: $[1,2]$ where $|x-2|=2-x$ and $[2,3]$ where $|x-2|=x-2$. The integral splits accordingly:

$\int_{1}^{3} |x-2| dx = \int_{1}^{2} (2-x) dx + \int_{2}^{3} (x-2) dx$

Evaluating the first integral:

$\int_{1}^{2} (2-x) dx = \left[2x - \frac{x^2}{2}\right]_{1}^{2} = (4-2) - \left(2 - \frac{1}{2}\right) = 2 - \frac{3}{2} = \frac{1}{2}$

The second integral yields:

$\int_{2}^{3} (x-2) dx = \left[\frac{x^2}{2} - 2x\right]_{2}^{3} = \left(\frac{9}{2}-6\right) - \left(\frac{4}{2}-4\right) = -\frac{3}{2} + 2 = \frac{1}{2}$

The total area is $\frac{1}{2} + \frac{1}{2} = 1$ square unit.

Geometrically, the region comprises two congruent right triangles with bases and heights of length $1$ each, confirming the area of $1$ square unit.

The area is $\boxed{A}$.

61295.subject: Mathematics
61295.text: The general solution of the differential equation $(x+y)\dfrac{dy}{dx} = 1$ is
options: $x + y + 1 = c$, where $c$ is a constant of integration
$x + y + 1 = ce^y$, where $c$ is a constant of integration
$x + y + 1 = ce^{-y}$, where $c$ is a constant of integration
$x + y - 1 = ce^{-y}$, where $c$ is a constant of integration
61295.sol:
Given differential equation is $(x+y)\dfrac{dy}{dx} = 1$

Rewriting the equation, we get $\dfrac{dx}{dy} = x + y$

$\dfrac{dx}{dy} - x = y$

This is a linear differential equation of the form $\dfrac{dx}{dy} + Px = Q$, where $P = -1$ and $Q = y$.

Integrating Factor (IF) $= e^{\int P dy} = e^{\int -1 dy} = e^{-y}$

The general solution is given by $x \cdot (\text{IF}) = \int Q \cdot (\text{IF}) dy + c$

$x e^{-y} = \int y e^{-y} dy + c$

Using integration by parts,

$x e^{-y} = y(-e^{-y}) - \int 1 \cdot (-e^{-y}) dy + c$

$x e^{-y} = -y e^{-y} - e^{-y} + c$

Multiplying both sides by $e^y$, we get

$x = -y - 1 + c e^y$

$x + y + 1 = c e^y$

Answer: $x + y + 1 = ce^y$, where $c$ is a constant of integration

The slope at any point $(x, y)$ is $\frac{dy}{dx} = 1 - \frac{1}{x^2}$. Integrating both sides with respect to $x$ yields $y = \int (1 - x^{-2})dx = x + x^{-1} + C$.

Given that the curve passes through $(2, \frac{9}{2})$, substitute to find $C$:

$\frac{9}{2} = 2 + \frac{1}{2} + C$

$C = 2$

The equation becomes $y = x + \frac{1}{x} + 2$. Multiplying through by $x$ gives $xy = x^2 + 1 + 2x = x^2 + 2x + 1$, which corresponds to option A.

Substituting the cosine rule expressions into the given equation:

$\cos A = \frac{b^2+c^2-a^2}{2bc}$, $\cos B = \frac{a^2+c^2-b^2}{2ac}$, $\cos C = \frac{a^2+b^2-c^2}{2ab}$

The right side simplifies to $\frac{a^2+b^2}{abc}$.

Equating both sides:

$\frac{a^2+3b^2+c^2}{2abc} = \frac{a^2+b^2}{abc}$

Multiplying through by $2abc$ and simplifying yields:

$b^2 + c^2 = a^2$

64265.text: If the vertices of a triangle are $(-2,3),(6,-1)$ and $(4,3)$, then the co-ordinates of the circumcentre of the triangle are
64265.sol:
Here, $\mathrm{A}(-2,3), \mathrm{B}(6,-1), \mathrm{C}(4,3)$ are the vertices of $\triangle \mathrm{ABC}$. Let $\mathrm{F}$ be the circumcentre of $\triangle \mathrm{ABC}$. Let $\mathrm{FD}$ and $\mathrm{FE}$ be the perpendicular bisectors of the sides $\mathrm{BC}$ and $\mathrm{AC}$ respectively. $\therefore \quad \mathrm{D}$ and $\mathrm{E}$ are the midpoints of side $\mathrm{BC}$ and $\mathrm{AC}$ respectively. $\begin{array}{ll}\therefore & D \equiv\left(\frac{6+4}{2}, \frac{-1+3}{2}\right) \\ \therefore & D=(5,1) \\ & \text{ and } E \equiv\left(\frac{-2+4}{2}, \frac{3+3}{2}\right)\end{array}$ $\therefore \quad \mathrm{E}=(1,3)$
Now, slope of $B C=\frac{3-(-1)}{4-6}=\frac{4}{-2}=-2$ $\therefore \quad \text{ Slope of } \mathrm{FD}=\frac{1}{2} \quad \ldots[\because \mathrm{FD} \perp \mathrm{BC}]$ Since FD passes through $(5,1)$ and has slope $\frac{1}{2}$, equation of $\mathrm{FD}$ is $\begin{aligned} & y-1=\frac{1}{2}(x-5) \\ \therefore \quad & 2(y-1)=x-5 \\ \therefore \quad & 2 y-2=x-5 \\ \therefore \quad & x-2 y-3=0 \end{aligned}$ Since both the points $\mathrm{A}$ and $\mathrm{C}$ have same $y$ co-ordinates i.e. 3 , the given points lie on the line $y=3$. Since the equation $\mathrm{FE}$ passes through $\mathrm{E}(1,3)$, the equation of $\mathrm{FE}$ is $x=1$. To find co-ordinates of circumcentre, we have to solve equations (i) and (ii). Substituting the value of $x$ in (i), we get $\begin{array}{ll} & 1-2 y-3=0 \\ \therefore \quad & y=-1 \\ \therefore \quad & \text{ Co-ordinates of circumcentre } \mathrm{F} \equiv(1,-1) . \end{array}$

64822.subject: Mathematics
64822.text: If the equation $\sin 3\theta - \cos^2\theta = \dfrac{1}{4}$ and $\theta \in [0, \pi]$, then the number of solutions is...
64822.sol:
Given equation: $\sin 3\theta - \cos^2\theta = \dfrac{1}{4}$

Using the identities $\sin 3\theta = 3\sin\theta - 4\sin^3\theta$ and $\cos^2\theta = 1 - \sin^2\theta$, we get:

$3\sin\theta - 4\sin^3\theta - (1 - \sin^2\theta) = \dfrac{1}{4}$

Multiplying by $4$ and rearranging the terms:

$12\sin\theta - 16\sin^3\theta - 4 + 4\sin^2\theta = 1$

$16\sin^3\theta - 4\sin^2\theta - 12\sin\theta + 5 = 0$

Let $\sin\theta = x$. Since $\theta \in [0, \pi]$, we must have $x \in [0, 1]$. The equation becomes:

$16x^3 - 4x^2 - 12x + 5 = 0$

By inspection, $x = \dfrac{1}{2}$ is a root. Factoring out $(2x - 1)$:

$(2x - 1)(8x^2 + 2x - 5) = 0$

The roots are $x = \dfrac{1}{2}$ and the solutions to $8x^2 + 2x - 5 = 0$. Using the quadratic formula:

$x = \dfrac{-2 \pm \sqrt{4 - 4(8)(-5)}}{16} = \dfrac{-2 \pm \sqrt{164}}{16} = \dfrac{-1 \pm \sqrt{41}}{8}$

Since $\sqrt{41} \approx 6.4$, the roots are approximately $x \approx 0.675$ and $x \approx -0.925$.

The valid values for $x = \sin\theta$ in the interval $[0, 1]$ are $x = \dfrac{1}{2}$ and $x = \dfrac{\sqrt{41} - 1}{8}$.

For each value of $\sin\theta \in (0, 1)$, there are exactly $2$ solutions in the interval $[0, \pi]$.

Therefore, the total number of solutions is $2 + 2 = 4$.

Answer: $4$

66055.subject: Physics
66055.text: If the charge on the capacitor is increased by 2C, the energy stored in it increases by $21 \%$. The original charge on the capacitor is
66055.sol:
The original charge $Q$ and capacitance $C$ yield stored energy $U = \frac{Q^2}{2C}$.

After adding $2\text{ C}$, the charge becomes $Q + 2$ and energy becomes $U' = \frac{(Q + 2)^2}{2C}$.

Given a $21\%$ energy increase, $U' = 1.21U$, so

\[$\frac{(Q + 2)^2}{2C} =$1.21 $\cdot \frac{Q^2}{2C}.$\]

Canceling $\frac{1}{2C}$ from both sides, $(Q + 2)^2 = 1.21Q^2$.

Solving this quadratic equation gives $Q + 2 = \pm 1.1Q$.

The positive case yields $Q = \frac{2}{0.1} = 20\text{ C}$, while the negative case gives $Q = -\frac{2}{2.1}\text{ C}$, which is discarded.

Final answer: $20\text{ C}$

The induced emf e $=\frac{\mathrm{d} \phi}{\mathrm{dt}}=\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{dt}}(\mathrm{AB})=\mathrm{B} \frac{\mathrm{dA}}{\mathrm{dt}}$
In one rotation the rod traces out a circle of radius 1 or an area $\mathrm{A}=\pi \mathrm{l}^2$
So, in $n$ rotations it will trace out an area of $n \pi l^2\begin{aligned} & \therefore \mathrm{e}=\mathrm{B} \frac{\Delta \mathrm{A}}{\Delta \mathrm{t}}=\mathrm{B} \cdot \frac{\mathrm{n} \pi \mathrm{l}^2}{\Delta \mathrm{t}} \\ & \text{ But } \frac{\mathrm{n}}{\Delta \mathrm{t}}=\frac{\text{ No.of rev.performed }}{\text{ time }}=\text{ frequency } \mathrm{f} \\ & \therefore \mathrm{e}=\mathrm{Bf} \pi \mathrm{l}^2=\text{ Bf.A } \\ & \therefore \mathrm{f}=\frac{\mathrm{e}}{\mathrm{B} \pi \mathrm{l}^2}\end{aligned}$

& \therefore \frac{1}{2} \mathrm{mV}^2=4 \mathrm{mV}_{\mathrm{e}^2 \\
& \therefore \mathrm{V}^2=8 \mathrm{ V}_{\mathrm{e}^2 \\
& \mathrm{ V}=2 \sqrt{2} \mathrm{ V}_{\mathrm{e}}
\end{aligned}$

67539.text:
A ball is dropped on the floor from a height of 20 m. It rebounds to a height of 5 m. Ball remains in contact with floor for 1 s. The average acceleration during contact is
(acceleration due to gravity $=10 \mathrm{ m} / \mathrm{s}^2$ )
67539.sol:
A ball dropped from $h_1 = 20\text{m}$ with $g = 10\text{m/s}^2$ reaches the ground with velocity $v_{\text{before}} = -\sqrt{2gh_1} = -\sqrt{2 \times 10 \times 20} = -20\text{m/s}$.

After rebounding to $h_2 = 5\text{m}$, its upward velocity is $v_{\text{after}} = \sqrt{2gh_2} = \sqrt{2 \times 10 \times 5} = 10\text{m/s}$.

During the $\Delta t = 1\text{s}$ contact, the average acceleration is
$a_{\text{avg}} = \frac{\Delta v}{\Delta t} = \frac{v_{\text{after}} - v_{\text{before}}}{\Delta t} = \frac{10 - (-20)}{1} = 30\text{m/s}^2$.

The average acceleration is $\boxed{\text{A}}$.

68721.sol:
Phase difference in SHM for given times

Given the period $T = 16\text{ s}$, angular frequency is $\omega = \frac{2\pi}{T} = \frac{\pi}{8}\text{ rad/s}$.

With times $t_1 = 2\text{ s}$ and $t_2 = 4\text{ s}$, the time difference is $\Delta t = t_2 - t_1 = 2\text{ s}$.

The phase difference is then $\Delta\phi = \omega \Delta t = \frac{\pi}{8} \times 2 = \frac{\pi}{4}\text{ rad}$.

The phase difference is $\frac{\pi}{4}\text{ rad}$, corresponding to choice C.

71458.subject: Biology
71458.text: In Yeast, the pyruvate is decarboxylated to form----
71458.sol:
In yeast, during anaerobic respiration (alcoholic fermentation), pyruvic acid undergoes incomplete oxidation in two steps.

First, pyruvic acid is decarboxylated to form acetaldehyde and carbon dioxide. This reaction is catalyzed by the enzyme pyruvate decarboxylase.

Second, acetaldehyde is reduced to ethyl alcohol (ethanol) by the enzyme alcohol dehydrogenase, utilizing NADH + H^{+}$.

Therefore, the direct product of the decarboxylation of pyruvate is acetaldehyde.

Answer: Acetaldehyde$

Aniline has the chemical formula $C_6H_5NH_2$.

The nitrogen atom of the amino group ($-NH_2$) is directly attached to only one carbon atom of the benzene ring, making it a primary (1^0$) amine.

72049.subject: Chemistry
72049.text: What is the enthalpy of formation of HF if bond enthalpies of H-H, F-F and H-F bonds are $434$ kJ/mol, $158$ kJ/mol and $565$ kJ/mol respectively. ?
72049.sol:
The reaction for the formation of $HF$ is:

$\dfrac{1}{2}H_2(g) + \dfrac{1}{2}F_2(g) \rightarrow HF(g)$

The enthalpy of formation is given by:

$\Delta_f H = \sum \text{Bond enthalpies of reactants} - \sum \text{Bond enthalpies of products}$

$\Delta_f H = \left[ \dfrac{1}{2} \times BE(H-H) + \dfrac{1}{2} \times BE(F-F) \right] - BE(H-F)$

Substituting the given values:

$\Delta_f H = \left[ \dfrac{1}{2}(434) + \dfrac{1}{2}(158) \right] - 565$

$\Delta_f H = (217 + 79) - 565$

$\Delta_f H = 296 - 565 = -269 \text{ kJ/mol}$

Answer: $-269$ kJ/mol

72460.subject: Physics
72460.text:
For Young's double slit experiment, two statements are given below.
Statement I: In the interference pattern, energy is not destroyed at the dark fringes; it is simply redistributed to the bright fringes.
Statement II: Fringe width (X) increases with the increase in frequency of light.
options: Statement I is false but statement II is true.
Statement I is false and statement II is false.
Statement I is true and statement II is true.
Statement I is true but statement II is false.
72460.sol:
Statement I is based on the principle of conservation of energy. In an interference pattern, the energy missing at dark fringes appears at the bright fringes. Thus, energy is only redistributed and not destroyed. Statement I is true.

The fringe width in Young's double slit experiment is given by $\beta = \dfrac{\lambda D}{d}$.

Since frequency $\nu = \dfrac{c}{\lambda}$, we have $\beta = \dfrac{c D}{\nu d}$.

This shows that fringe width is inversely proportional to the frequency of light. Therefore, as frequency increases, fringe width decreases. Statement II is false.

Hence, Statement I is true but Statement II is false.

Answer: Statement I is true but statement II is false.

72492.subject: Physics
72492.text:
Four harmonics of equal frequencies and equal intensities $I_0$ have phase angles $0, \dfrac{\pi}{3}, \dfrac{2\pi}{3}, \pi$. When they are superimposed, the intensity of the resultant wave is "$nI_0$". The value of n is
(all phase angles are in radian and $\cos(60)^{}^{\circ} = \dfrac{1}{2}$)
72492.sol:
Let the amplitude of each harmonic wave be $A_0$. The intensity of each wave is $I_0 = k A_0^2$.

The waves can be represented as vectors (phasors) with magnitudes $A_0$ and angles $0, \dfrac{\pi}{3}, \dfrac{2\pi}{3}, \pi$.

The x-component of the resultant amplitude is:
$A_x = A_0 \cos(0) + A_0 \cos\left(\dfrac{\pi}{3}\right) + A_0 \cos\left(\dfrac{2\pi}{3}\right) + A_0 \cos(\pi)$
$A_x = A_0 \left( 1 + \dfrac{1}{2} - \dfrac{1}{2} - 1 \right) = 0$

The y-component of the resultant amplitude is:
$A_y = A_0 \sin(0) + A_0 \sin\left(\dfrac{\pi}{3}\right) + A_0 \sin\left(\dfrac{2\pi}{3}\right) + A_0 \sin(\pi)$
$A_y = A_0 \left( 0 + \dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2} + \dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2} + 0 \right) = \sqrt{3} A_0$

The resultant amplitude $A_R$ is given by:
$A_R = \sqrt{A_x^2 + A_y^2} = \sqrt{0 + (\sqrt{3} A_0)^2} = \sqrt{3} A_0$

The resultant intensity $I_R$ is proportional to the square of the resultant amplitude:
$I_R = k A_R^2 = k (\sqrt{3} A_0)^2 = 3 k A_0^2 = 3 I_0$

Comparing this with $n I_0$, we get $n = 3$.

Answer: $3$

73792.subject: General Ability
73792.text:
Two forces of equal magnitude simultaneously act at a point. It is observed that the resultant force is equal in magnitude to the individual forces. Which of the following statements is/are correct?
I. The angle between one of the individual forces and the resultant force is $\pi/3$.
II. The angle between the individual forces is $2\pi/3$.
73792.sol:
Let the two forces be $\vec{F_1}$ and $\vec{F_2}$, and their resultant be $\vec{R}$.

Given that $|\vec{F_1}| = |\vec{F_2}| = |\vec{R}| = F$.

The magnitude of the resultant of two vectors is given by $R^2 = F_1^2 + F_2^2 + 2F_1 F_2 \cos \theta$, where $\theta$ is the angle between the two forces.

Substituting the given values:

$F^2 = F^2 + F^2 + 2F^2 \cos \theta$

$F^2 = 2F^2(1 + \cos \theta)$

$\cos \theta = -\dfrac{1}{2}$

$\theta = \dfrac{2\pi}{3}$

Thus, the angle between the individual forces is $\dfrac{2\pi}{3}$. Statement II is correct.

Since the two forces are equal in magnitude, their resultant bisects the angle between them. Let $\alpha$ be the angle between the resultant and one of the forces.

$\alpha = \dfrac{\theta}{2} = \dfrac{1}{2} \left(\dfrac{2\pi}{3}\right) = \dfrac{\pi}{3}$

Thus, the angle between one of the individual forces and the resultant force is $\dfrac{\pi}{3}$. Statement I is also correct.

Both statements I and II are correct.

They provide flexibility to plant due to their thickened walls
These are present in the bark of a tree only
Growth occurs in plants due to division of cells of these tissues
74416.sol: Meristematic tissues, or simply meristems, are tissues in which the cells remain forever young and divide actively throughout the life of the plant. Cells within the meristematic tissues are self-renewing, so that each time they divide, one cell remains identical to the parent while the other can specialize and become part of another plant structure. The meristematic tissue is therefore self-sustaining.

78332.subject: Mathematics
78332.text: If $p^{\text{th}}$ term of an AP is $k$, then what is the sum of $p^{\text{th}}$ term, $(p+q)^{\text{th}}$ term and $(p-q)^{\text{th}}$ term of the AP ?
78332.sol:
Let the first term of the AP be $a$ and the common difference be $d$.

The $p^{\text{th}}$ term is given by $T_p = a + (p-1)d = k$.

The $(p+q)^{\text{th}}$ term is $T_{p+q} = a + (p+q-1)d$.

The $(p-q)^{\text{th}}$ term is $T_{p-q} = a + (p-q-1)d$.

The required sum is $T_p + T_{p+q} + T_{p-q}$.

Substituting the values, we get:

$[a + (p-1)d] + [a + (p+q-1)d] + [a + (p-q-1)d]$

$= 3a + d[(p-1) + (p+q-1) + (p-q-1)]$

$= 3a + d(3p - 3)$

$= 3[a + (p-1)d]$

Since $a + (p-1)d = k$, the sum is $3k$.

Answer: $3k$

79470.subject: Botany
79470.text: In the case of Poriferans, the spongocoel is lined with flagellated cells called
79470.sol: Choanocytes (collar cells) form the lining of spongocoel in poriferans (sponges). Flagella in collar cells provide circulation to water in the water canal system. These distinctive cells line the interior body walls of sponges. These cells have a central flagellum that is surrounded by a collar of microvilli. Choanocytes are versatile cells. Their flagella beat to create the active pumping of water through the sponge, while the collars of the choanocytes are the primary areas where nutrients are absorbed into the sponge. Furthermore, in some sponges, the choanocytes develop into gametes.

80194.subject: Botany
80194.text: The $\mathrm{C}_4$-plants are photosynthetically more efficient than $\mathrm{C}_3$-plants because
options: $\mathrm{CO}_2$ generated during photorespiration is trapped and recycled through PEP carboxylase
80194.sol:
$\mathrm{C}_4$-plants show Kranz anatomy. In the leaves of $\mathrm{C}_4$-plants, the vascular bundles are surrounded by bundle sheath of parenchymatous cells, which in turn are surrounded by mesophyll cells. Chloroplasts in bundle sheath cells are larger and always contain grana whereas chloroplasts in mesophyll cells are smaller. The $\mathrm{C}_4$-plants are photosynthetically more efficient than $\mathrm{C}_3$-plants because they have more chloroplasts.
Photorespiration takes place only in $\mathrm{C}_3$-plants. It occurs in chlorophyllous tíssue. At high temperature and high oxygen concentration the affinity of RuBP carboxylase for $\mathrm{CO}_2$ decrease and for $\mathrm{O}_2$ increases.
Photosynthesis takes $\mathrm{CO}_2$ and release $\mathrm{O}_2$, while respiration utilizes $\mathrm{O}_2$ and release $\mathrm{CO}_2$. If the light factor is saturating, there will be certain concentration of $\mathrm{CO}_2$ in the atmosphere at which the rate of photosynthesis will be equal to rate of respiration. This is called carbon dioxide compensation point. $\mathrm{C}_4$-plants have very low $\mathrm{CO}_2$ compensation point

80283.subject: Botany
80283.text: Fruit and leaf drop at early stages can be prevented by the application of
80283.sol:
Among the various types of growth promoters in plants, Auxins, Gibberellins and Cytokinins are most common and well characterized. The Auxin delay abscission of leaves and fruits at early stages. Whenever leaf or fruit fall occurs, the organ concerned stops producing auxin. However, it promotes abscission of order, mature leaves, and fruit. Abscision is a natural phenomenon of old parts. Primarily this is accomplished by Abscisic acid hormone (ABA). NAA prevents fruit drop in tomato; 2,4-D prevents fruit drop in Citrus.

Cytokinins are mainly involved in cell division. Gibberellins are mainly involved in stem internode elongation.

According to Darwin's theory of natural selection, The individual possessing useful variations survive whereas the others are eliminated. Nature selects the best suited and discards the others (survival of the fittest). Pesticide resistant insects are selected over pesticide sensitive insects by nature, and are thus survive through the course of evolution, until more suited (fittest) individual is selected, eliminating the former.
Related Theory
Darwinism can explain the survival of fittest but is unable to account for arrival of the fittest. It is difficult to suppose that small variations could have formed organs like wings and mimicry colouration which are useful only in their fully developed state but what about their presence in early stages.

98425.sol:
Enzymes are composed of one or several polypeptide chains. However, there are a number of cases in which non-protein constituents called cofactors are bound to the the enzyme to make the enzyme catalytically active.&
In these instances, the protein portion of the enzymes is called the apoenzyme. Three kinds of cofactors may be identified: prosthetic groups, co-enzymes and metal ions.
A number of enzymes require metal ions for their activity which form coordination bonds with side chains at the active site and at the same time form one or more cordination bonds with the substrate, e.g., zinc is a cofactor for the proteolytic enzyme carboxypeptidase.

102409.subject: Physics
102409.text: A block of mass $m$ is connected to two identical massless springs, each of spring constant $k$. In the first case, the two springs are connected in series. In the second case, they are connected in parallel. If the block is given the same amplitude of oscillation in both cases, what is the ratio of its maximum speed in the first case to its maximum speed in the second case?
102409.sol:
The maximum speed of a block in simple harmonic motion is given by $v_{\max} = A\omega = A\sqrt{\dfrac{k_{\text{eq}}}{m}}$.

In the first case, the springs are in series. The equivalent spring constant is $k_{\text{series}} = \dfrac{k \times k}{k + k} = \dfrac{k}{2}$.

In the second case, the springs are in parallel. The equivalent spring constant is $k_{\text{parallel}} = k + k = 2k$.

Since the amplitude $A$ and mass $m$ are the same in both cases, the maximum speed is directly proportional to $\sqrt{k_{\text{eq}}}$.

Therefore, the ratio of the maximum speeds is:
$\dfrac{v_{\text{series}}}{v_{\text{parallel}}} = \sqrt{\dfrac{k_{\text{series}}}{k_{\text{parallel}}}} = \sqrt{\dfrac{k/2}{2k}} = \sqrt{\dfrac{1}{4}} = \dfrac{1}{2}$.

The ratio is $1 : 2$.

Answer: $1 : 2$

As the bridge is balanced, hence it is balanced Wheatstone's bridge.

\text{ or } & & \frac{2}{2} & =\frac{2(6+S)}{6 S} \\
\text{ or } & & 3 S  & =6+S \\
\text{ or } & & S & =3 \Omega
\end{aligned}$

103539.subject: Physics
103539.text: A thin straight bar magnet has a magnetic moment $M$. It is bent at its exact midpoint to form a V-shape such that the angle between the two halves is $60^{\circ}$. The new magnetic moment of the magnet is
103539.sol:
Let the initial length of the bar magnet be $L$ and its pole strength be $m$.

The initial magnetic moment is $M = m \times L$.

When the magnet is bent at its midpoint, each half has a length of $\dfrac{L}{2}$.

The angle between the two halves is $60^{\circ}$.

The new effective magnetic length $L^{\prime}$ is the shortest straight-line distance between the two poles.

The two halves and the line joining the poles form a triangle with two equal sides ($\dfrac{L}{2}$) and an included angle of $60^{\circ}$. This geometry forms an equilateral triangle.

Therefore, the distance between the poles is $L^{\prime} = \dfrac{L}{2}$.

The new magnetic moment is $M^{\prime} = m \times L^{\prime} = m \times \left(\dfrac{L}{2}\right) = \dfrac{M}{2}$.

Answer: $\dfrac{M}{2}$

104122.subject: Physics
104122.text: A series LCR circuit is connected to an AC source of variable frequency. At a particular frequency, the current in the circuit is in phase with the applied voltage. If the inductive reactance at this frequency is $50\ \Omega$ and the capacitance of the circuit is $20\ \mu\text{F}$, the frequency of the AC source is :
104122.sol:
The current is in phase with the voltage when the circuit is at resonance.

At resonance, the inductive reactance ($X_L$) equals the capacitive reactance ($X_C$):

$X_L = X_C$

Given $X_L = 50\ \Omega$, we have $X_C = 50\ \Omega$.

The capacitive reactance is given by $X_C = \dfrac{1}{\omega C}$.

Substituting the given values ($C = 20\ \mu\text{F} = 20 \times 10^{-6}\text{ F}$):

$50 = \dfrac{1}{\omega \times 20 \times 10^{-6}}$

$\omega = \dfrac{1}{50 \times 20 \times 10^{-6}} = \dfrac{1}{1000 \times 10^{-6}} = \dfrac{1}{10^{-3}} = 1000\text{ rad/s}$

The linear frequency $f$ is related to the angular frequency $\omega$ by $f = \dfrac{\omega}{2\pi}$:

$f = \dfrac{1000}{2\pi} = \dfrac{500}{\pi}\text{ Hz}$

Answer: $\dfrac{500}{\pi}\text{ Hz}$

104279.text: An electromagnetic wave is found to have a wavelength of the order of $1\text{ \AA}$ ($10^{-10}\text{ m}$). Identify the electromagnetic wave and the standard method used to produce it.
options: X-rays; produced by bombarding a metal target with high energy electrons.
Gamma rays; produced by the radioactive decay of the nucleus.
Ultraviolet rays; produced by special lamps and very hot bodies.
X-rays; produced by the vibration of atoms and molecules.
104279.sol:
The wavelength of $1\text{ \AA}$ ($10^{-10}\text{ m}$) falls in the characteristic range of X-rays, which typically span from $10^{-8}\text{ m}$ to $10^{-13}\text{ m}$.

According to the electromagnetic spectrum, X-rays are commonly produced by bombarding a metal target with high energy electrons.

Gamma rays generally have even shorter wavelengths and are of nuclear origin. Ultraviolet rays have longer wavelengths ($10^{-8}\text{ m}$ to $4 \times 10^{-7}\text{ m}$). The vibration of atoms and molecules produces infrared waves, not X-rays.

Answer: X-rays; produced by bombarding a metal target with high energy electrons.

104682.subject: Physics
104682.text: A beam of unpolarized light travels from a denser medium of refractive index $\mu_1$ to a rarer medium of refractive index $\mu_2$. If $i_p$ is the polarizing angle (Brewster's angle) for this interface, then which of the following is the correct range for $i_p$?
options: The polarizing angle does not exist for light traveling from a denser to a rarer medium
104682.sol:
According to Brewster's law, when light travels from a medium of refractive index $\mu_1$ to a medium of refractive index $\mu_2$, the polarizing angle $i_p$ is given by $\tan(i_p) = \dfrac{\mu_2}{\mu_1}$.

Since the light is traveling from a denser medium to a rarer medium, we have $\mu_1 > \mu_2$.

This implies that the relative refractive index $\dfrac{\mu_2}{\mu_1} < 1$.

Therefore, $\tan(i_p) < 1$.

Since $i_p$ must be a positive angle, and $\tan(45^\circ) = 1$, the polarizing angle must lie in the range $0^\circ < i_p < 45^\circ$.

Answer: $0^\circ < i_p < 45^\circ$

106409.subject: Chemistry
106409.text: The radius of the first Bohr orbit of a hydrogen atom is $a_0$. The de Broglie wavelength of an electron in the third Bohr orbit of a $\text{He}^+$ ion is:
106409.sol:
The radius of the $n^{\text{th}}$ Bohr orbit is given by $r_n = a_0 \dfrac{n^2}{Z}$.

For the $3^{\text{rd}}$ orbit of $\text{He}^+$ ($n = 3, Z = 2$):
$r_3 = a_0 \dfrac{3^2}{2} = 4.5 a_0$

According to de Broglie's hypothesis and Bohr's quantization condition, the circumference of the orbit is equal to an integral multiple of the de Broglie wavelength ($\lambda$):
$2\pi r_n = n\lambda$

Substituting the values:
$2\pi (4.5 a_0) = 3\lambda$
$9\pi a_0 = 3\lambda$
$\lambda = 3\pi a_0$

Alternatively, using $\lambda = \dfrac{2\pi a_0 n}{Z}$, we get $\lambda = \dfrac{2\pi a_0 (3)}{2} = 3\pi a_0$.

Answer: $3 \pi a_0$

107009.chapter: Classification of Elements and Periodicity in Properties
107009.text:
Match the compounds in List I with their dominant redox behaviour in List II based on the inert pair effect.

List IList II
A. $\text{PbO}_2$I. Strong reducing agent
B. $\text{SnCl}_2$II. Strong oxidizing agent (due to $+4 \rightarrow +2$ transition)
C. $\text{TlCl}_3$III. Strong oxidizing agent (due to $+3 \rightarrow +1$ transition)
D. $\text{AlCl}_3$IV. Highly stable in its current oxidation state

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
107009.sol:
The inert pair effect causes the lower oxidation state to become more stable down the group in p-block elements.

A. $\text{PbO}_2$: Pb is in the $+4$ state. Since $+2$ is more stable for the heavier Pb, it readily accepts electrons to form $\text{Pb}^{2+}$, acting as a strong oxidizing agent (Match II).

B. $\text{SnCl}_2$: Sn is in the $+2$ state. Since $+4$ is more stable for the lighter Sn, it readily loses electrons to form $\text{Sn}^{4+}$, acting as a strong reducing agent (Match I).

C. $\text{TlCl}_3$: Tl is in the $+3$ state. Since $+1$ is more stable for the heavier Tl, it readily accepts electrons to form $\text{Tl}^{+}$, acting as a strong oxidizing agent (Match III).

D. $\text{AlCl}_3$: Al is in the $+3$ state, which is its most stable oxidation state, so it does not act as a strong oxidizing or reducing agent (Match IV).

Therefore, the correct match is A-II, B-I, C-III, D-IV.

Answer: A-II, B-I, C-III, D-IV

107781.subject: Chemistry
107781.text:
Given below are two statements: one is labelled as Assertion (A) and the other is labelled as Reason (R).

Assertion (A): The molecule $\text{ClF}_3$ has a bent T-shape geometry.
Reason (R): In $\text{ClF}_3$, the central chlorine atom is $sp^3d$ hybridized and its two lone pairs occupy axial positions to minimize repulsion.

In the light of the above statements, choose the most appropriate answer from the options given below:
options: Both (A) and (R) are correct and (R) is the correct explanation of (A)
Both (A) and (R) are correct but (R) is not the correct explanation of (A)
(A) is correct but (R) is not correct
(A) is not correct but (R) is correct
107781.sol:
For $\text{ClF}_3$, the central $\text{Cl}$ atom has $7$ valence electrons. It forms $3$ single bonds with $\text{F}$ atoms and has $2$ lone pairs. The steric number is $3 + 2 = 5$, which corresponds to $sp^3d$ hybridization and a trigonal bipyramidal electron geometry.

According to VSEPR theory, lone pairs occupy the equatorial positions in a trigonal bipyramidal geometry to minimize repulsions, as equatorial positions experience fewer $90^\circ$ repulsions compared to axial positions. Placing the two lone pairs in equatorial positions results in a bent T-shape molecular geometry. Therefore, Assertion (A) is correct.

Reason (R) is incorrect because the lone pairs occupy equatorial positions, not axial positions.

Answer: (A) is correct but (R) is not correct

108658.subject: Chemistry
108658.text:
Given below are two statements: one is labelled as Assertion (A) and the other is labelled as Reason (R).

Assertion (A): Given $\Delta H_f^\circ(\mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{O}(l)) = -286 \text{ kJ mol}^{-1}$ and $\Delta H_f^\circ(\mathrm{OH}^-(aq)) = -230 \text{ kJ mol}^{-1}$, the standard enthalpy of neutralization of a strong acid and strong base is $-56 \text{ kJ mol}^{-1}$.
Reason (R): The standard enthalpy of formation of $\mathrm{H}^+(aq)$ is taken as zero by convention.

In the light of the above statements, choose the most appropriate answer from the options given below:
options: Both Assertion and Reason are true but Reason is not the correct explanation of Assertion.
Both Assertion and Reason are true and Reason is the correct explanation of Assertion.
Assertion is true but Reason is false.
Assertion is false but Reason is true.
108658.sol:
The net ionic equation for the neutralization of a strong acid and a strong base is:
$\mathrm{H}^+(aq) + \mathrm{OH}^-(aq) \rightarrow \mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{O}(l)$

The standard enthalpy of neutralization is calculated using Hess's Law:
$\Delta H_{neut}^\circ = \Delta H_f^\circ(\mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{O}(l)) - [\Delta H_f^\circ(\mathrm{H}^+(aq)) + \Delta H_f^\circ(\mathrm{OH}^-(aq))]$

By IUPAC convention, the standard enthalpy of formation of the aqueous hydrogen ion, $\mathrm{H}^+(aq)$, is assigned a value of zero at all temperatures. Thus, the Reason is true.

Substituting the given values:
$\Delta H_{neut}^\circ = -286 - [0 + (-230)] = -286 + 230 = -56 \text{ kJ mol}^{-1}$

The Assertion is true, and the calculation explicitly relies on the convention stated in the Reason. Therefore, the Reason is the correct explanation of the Assertion.

Answer: Both Assertion and Reason are true and Reason is the correct explanation of Assertion.

108683.subject: Chemistry
108683.text: In which of the following physical processes is the change in entropy ($\Delta S$) positive?
options: Crystallization of sugar from a supersaturated solution
Condensation of steam to liquid water
108683.sol:
Entropy is a measure of the degree of randomness or disorder in a system.

When solid $\text{NaCl}$ dissolves in water, the highly ordered crystal lattice breaks down into free-moving $\text{Na}^{+}$ and $\text{Cl}^{-}$ ions in the solution, which increases the randomness. Hence, $\Delta S > 0$.

For the dissolution of $\text{CO}_{2}$ gas in water, the gaseous molecules are confined to the liquid phase, decreasing randomness ($\Delta S < 0$).

Crystallization of sugar involves the formation of an ordered solid from a solution, decreasing randomness ($\Delta S < 0$).

Condensation of steam converts a gas into a liquid, which also decreases randomness ($\Delta S < 0$).

Answer: Dissolution of solid $\text{NaCl}$ in water

114344.subject: Chemistry
114344.text: The molar conductivity of a $0.018 \text{ mol L}^{-1}$ solution of acetic acid is $39.05 \text{ S cm}^2 \text{ mol}^{-1}$. If the limiting molar conductivities of $\text{H}^+$ and $\text{CH}_3\text{COO}^-$ ions are $349.6 \text{ S cm}^2 \text{ mol}^{-1}$ and $40.9 \text{ S cm}^2 \text{ mol}^{-1}$ respectively, the acid dissociation constant ($K_a$) of acetic acid is:
114344.sol:
Limiting molar conductivity of acetic acid is:

$\Lambda_m^\circ = \lambda^\circ(\text{H}^+) + \lambda^\circ(\text{CH}_3\text{COO}^-)$
$\Lambda_m^\circ = 349.6 + 40.9 = 390.5 \text{ S cm}^2 \text{ mol}^{-1}$

Degree of dissociation, $\alpha = \dfrac{\Lambda_m}{\Lambda_m^\circ} = \dfrac{39.05}{390.5} = 0.1$

Using Ostwald's dilution law, the acid dissociation constant $K_a$ is:
$K_a = \dfrac{C\alpha^2}{1 - \alpha}$
$K_a = \dfrac{0.018 \times (0.1)^2}{1 - 0.1}$
$K_a = \dfrac{0.018 \times 0.01}{0.9} = \dfrac{1.8 \times 10^{-4}}{0.9} = 2.0 \times 10^{-4}$

Answer: $2.0 \times 10^{-4}$

114403.subject: Chemistry
114403.text:
A galvanic cell consists of a Standard Hydrogen Electrode (SHE) as the cathode and another hydrogen electrode ($P_{\text{H}_2} = 1$ atm) dipped in an unknown acidic solution as the anode. If the measured cell potential is $0.236$ V at $298$ K, what is the pH of the unknown solution?
$\left(\text{Given}: \dfrac{2.303\ RT}{F} = 0.059\right)$
114403.sol:
The cell can be represented as:
$\text{Pt (s)} | \text{H}_2 \text{(g, 1 atm)} | \text{H}^{+} \text{(aq, unknown)} \ || \ \text{H}^{+} \text{(aq, 1 M)} | \text{H}_2 \text{(g, 1 atm)} | \text{Pt (s)}$

The cell potential is given by:
$E_{\text{cell}} = E_{\text{cathode}} - E_{\text{anode}}$

For the Standard Hydrogen Electrode (cathode):
$E_{\text{cathode}} = 0$ V

For the anode (reduction potential):
$E_{\text{anode}} = E^{\circ}_{\text{H}^{+}/\text{H}_2} - \dfrac{0.059}{2} \log \dfrac{P_{\text{H}_2}}{[\text{H}^{+}]^2}$
$E_{\text{anode}} = 0 - \dfrac{0.059}{2} \log \dfrac{1}{[\text{H}^{+}]^2}$
$E_{\text{anode}} = - \dfrac{0.059}{2} \times (-2 \log [\text{H}^{+}])$
$E_{\text{anode}} = 0.059 \log [\text{H}^{+}] = -0.059 \text{ pH}$

Substituting into the cell potential equation:
$E_{\text{cell}} = 0 - (-0.059 \text{ pH}) = 0.059 \text{ pH}$

Given $E_{\text{cell}} = 0.236$ V:
$0.236 = 0.059 \text{ pH}$
$\text{pH} = \dfrac{0.236}{0.059} = 4$

Using $\dfrac{0.059}{2}$ directly for the pH relation leads to an incorrect pH of 8, and a sign error leads to -4.

Answer: $4$

114869.subject: Chemistry
114869.text:
The gas-phase decomposition of sulfuryl chloride is a first-order reaction:
$\text{SO}_2\text{Cl}_2(g) \rightarrow \text{SO}_2(g) + \text{Cl}_2(g)$

The initial pressure of $\text{SO}_2\text{Cl}_2$ is $0.5 \text{ atm}$. After $100 \text{ s}$, the total pressure of the reaction mixture becomes $0.75 \text{ atm}$. The rate constant for the reaction is:
114869.sol:
For the first-order gas-phase reaction:
$\text{SO}_2\text{Cl}_2(g) \rightarrow \text{SO}_2(g) + \text{Cl}_2(g)$

Let the initial pressure be $P_i$ and the decrease in pressure at time $t$ be $x$.
At $t = 0$: $P_i$, $0$, $0$
At $t = 100 \text{ s}$: $P_i - x$, $x$, $x$

Total pressure at time $t$, $P_t = (P_i - x) + x + x = P_i + x$
Therefore, $x = P_t - P_i$

The partial pressure of the reactant at time $t$ is:
$P_A = P_i - x = P_i - (P_t - P_i) = 2P_i - P_t$

Given $P_i = 0.5 \text{ atm}$ and $P_t = 0.75 \text{ atm}$:
$P_A = 2(0.5) - 0.75 = 1.0 - 0.75 = 0.25 \text{ atm}$

The first-order rate constant is:
$k = \dfrac{2.303}{t} \log\dfrac{P_i}{P_A}$

$k = \dfrac{2.303}{100} \log\dfrac{0.5}{0.25} = \dfrac{2.303}{100} \log 2$

$k = \dfrac{2.303 \times 0.3010}{100} = \dfrac{0.693}{100} = 6.93 \times 10^{-3} \text{ s}^{-1}$

Answer: $6.93 \times 10^{-3} \text{ s}^{-1}$
114869.meta: The gas-phase decomposition of sulfuryl chloride is a first-order reaction: SO_2Cl_2(g) arrow SO_2(g) + Cl_2(g) The initial pressure of SO_2Cl_2 is 0.5 atm .

114901.subject: Chemistry
114901.text: The decomposition of nitrous oxide, $2\text{N}_2\text{O}(g) \rightarrow 2\text{N}_2(g) + \text{O}_2(g)$, follows zero-order kinetics. If the initial concentration of $\text{N}_2\text{O}$ is $0.5$ M and the rate constant $k$ is $1.25 \times 10^{-3}$ M s$^{-1}$, what is the exact time taken for the reaction to reach $100\%$ completion?
114901.sol:
For the zero-order reaction $2\text{N}_2\text{O} \rightarrow 2\text{N}_2 + \text{O}_2$, the rate of reaction is expressed as:

$\text{Rate} = -\dfrac{1}{2}\dfrac{d[\text{N}_2\text{O}]}{dt} = k$

$\Rightarrow -\dfrac{d[\text{N}_2\text{O}]}{dt} = 2k$

The integrated rate law is:

$[\text{N}_2\text{O}]_0 - [\text{N}_2\text{O}]_t = 2kt$

For $100\%$ completion, the final concentration of the reactant is zero ($[\text{N}_2\text{O}]_t = 0$).

Substituting the given values ($[\text{N}_2\text{O}]_0 = 0.5$ M, $k = 1.25 \times 10^{-3}$ M s$^{-1}$):

$0.5 - 0 = 2 \times (1.25 \times 10^{-3}) \times t$

$0.5 = 2.5 \times 10^{-3} \times t$

$t = \dfrac{0.5}{2.5 \times 10^{-3}} = \dfrac{500}{2.5} = 200$ s

Omitting the stoichiometric factor of $2$ in the rate equation leads to the incorrect time of $400$ s.

Answer: $200$ s

115317.subject: Chemistry
115317.text:
Match List-I and List-II

List-I List-II
A. Osmosis I. Solvent molecules pass through semi permeable membrane towards solvent side.
B. Reverse osmosis II. Movement of charged colloidal particles under the influence of applied electric potential towards oppositely charged electrodes
C. Electro osmosis III. Solvent molecules pass through semi permeable membrane towards solution side
D. Electrophoresis IV. Dispersion medium moves in an electric field.

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
115317.sol:
(A) Osmosis: It is a process by which the molecules of a solvent pass from a solution of low concentration to a solution of high concentration through a semi-permeable membrane.

(B) Reverse osmosis: The direction of osmosis can be reversed if a pressure larger than the osmotic pressure is applied to the solution side. Now the pure solvent flows out of the solution through the semi-permeable membrane. This phenomenon is called reverse osmosis.

(C) Electroosmosis: When electrophoresis, i.e., movement of particles is prevented by some suitable means, it is observed that the dispersion medium begins to move in an electric field. This phenomenon is termed electroosmosis.

(D) Electrophoresis: When an electric potential is applied across two platinum electrodes dipping in a colloidal solution, the colloidal particles move towards one or the other electrode. The movement of colloidal particles under an applied electric potential is called electrophoresis.

So the correct matching is A-III, B-I, C-IV, D-II.

117782.subject: Chemistry
117782.text: An octahedral complex with the formula $[\text{M(H}_2\text{O})_6]^{2+}$ has a spin-only magnetic moment of approximately $3.87\text{ BM}$. Identify the central metal ion $\text{M}$ from the following options:
117782.sol:
The spin-only magnetic moment ($\mu$) is given by the formula $\mu = \sqrt{n(n+2)}\text{ BM}$, where $n$ is the number of unpaired electrons.

Given $\mu \approx 3.87\text{ BM}$, we can find $n$:
$\sqrt{n(n+2)} = 3.87$
$n(n+2) \approx 15$
This gives $n = 3$ unpaired electrons.

In the complex $[\text{M(H}_2\text{O})_6]^{2+}$, the metal ion $\text{M}$ is in the $+2$ oxidation state. Since $\text{H}_2\text{O}$ acts as a weak field ligand for most $+2$ metal ions, the complex will be high-spin. We evaluate the $3d$ electron configurations for the $+2$ ions of the given options in a high-spin octahedral field:

Chromium ($\text{Cr}^{2+}$): $3d^4$. High-spin configuration is $t_{2g}^3 e_g^1$, which has $4$ unpaired electrons.
Cobalt ($\text{Co}^{2+}$): $3d^7$. High-spin configuration is $t_{2g}^5 e_g^2$, which has $3$ unpaired electrons.
Manganese ($\text{Mn}^{2+}$): $3d^5$. High-spin configuration is $t_{2g}^3 e_g^2$, which has $5$ unpaired electrons.
Iron ($\text{Fe}^{2+}$): $3d^6$. High-spin configuration is $t_{2g}^4 e_g^2$, which has $4$ unpaired electrons.

Since $\text{Co}^{2+}$ has exactly $3$ unpaired electrons, the central metal ion $\text{M}$ is Cobalt.

Answer: Cobalt
